claim: The bacterial Sec translocon is a multi-protein complex responsible for translocating diverse proteins across the plasma membrane.
source: The bacterial Sec translocon is a multi-protein complex responsible for translocating diverse proteins across the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is a foundational statement about the Sec translocon that draws from established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: For post-translational protein translocation, the Sec-channel – SecYEG – associates with the motor protein SecA to mediate the ATP-dependent transport of pre-proteins across the membrane.
source: For post-translational protein translocation, the Sec-channel – SecYEG – associates with the motor protein SecA to mediate the ATP-dependent transport of pre-proteins across the membrane.
evidence: This statement describes the established mechanism of the Sec system, drawing from scientific knowledge.

claim: A diffusional-based Brownian ratchet mechanism for protein secretion has been previously proposed.
source: Previously, a diffusional-based Brownian ratchet mechanism for protein secretion has been proposed
evidence: This refers to prior work in the field, indicating citation-based support.

claim: The structural dynamics required to facilitate the Brownian ratchet mechanism remain unknown.
source: the structural dynamics required to facilitate this mechanism remain unknown.
evidence: This statement identifies a knowledge gap, based on inference from the existing literature.

claim: HDX-MS reveals striking nucleotide-dependent conformational changes in the Sec protein-channel from Escherichia coli.
source: Here, we employ hydrogen-deuterium exchange mass spectrometry (HDX-MS) to reveal striking nucleotide-dependent conformational changes in the Sec protein-channel from Escherichia coli.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the HDX-MS experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: ATP-dependent opening of SecY has been reported previously.
source: In addition to the ATP-dependent opening of SecY, reported previously
evidence: This refers to prior published work, indicating citation-based support.

claim: ATP-dependent constriction of SecA around the pre-protein occurs.
source: we observe a counteracting, and ATP-dependent, constriction of SecA around the pre-protein.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by HDX-MS data.

claim: ATP binding causes SecY to open and SecA to close.
source: ATP binding causes SecY to open and SecA to close
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by the HDX-MS experimental data.

claim: ADP produced by hydrolysis causes SecY to close and SecA to open.
source: while, ADP produced by hydrolysis, has the opposite effect.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by the HDX-MS experimental data.

claim: The alternating behavior of SecA and SecY could help impose the directionality of the Brownian ratchet for protein transport through the Sec machinery.
source: This alternating behaviour could help impose the directionality of the Brownian ratchet for protein transport through the Sec machinery.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: The Sec translocon is ubiquitous in the plasma membrane of bacteria and the endoplasmic reticulum of eukaryotes.
source: The ubiquitous Sec translocon performs this task in the plasma membrane of bacteria and the endoplasmic reticulum of eukaryotes.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the distribution of the Sec translocon.

claim: A protein-channel through the membrane is formed by the conserved hetero-trimeric core-complex: Sec61αβγ in eukaryotes, and SecYEG in archaea and bacteria.
source: A protein-channel through the membrane is formed by the conserved hetero-trimeric core-complex: Sec61αβγ in eukaryotes, and SecYEG in archaea and bacteria (Hartmann et al., 1994).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: In bacteria, protein secretion is important for cell envelope biogenesis and maintenance, as well as for the delivery of adherence and pathogenic effector proteins to the cell surface.
source: In bacteria, protein secretion is important for cell envelope biogenesis and maintenance, as well as for the delivery of adherence and pathogenic effector proteins to the cell surface.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about bacterial protein secretion.

claim: During protein secretion, SecYEG engages with the cytosolic motor ATPase SecA.
source: During protein secretion, SecYEG engages with the cytosolic motor ATPase SecA (Lill et al., 1989)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: SecA and SecYEG together pass pre-proteins with a short N-terminal cleavable signal sequence across the membrane, whilst still in an unfolded conformation.
source: and together they pass pre-proteins with a short N-terminal cleavable signal sequence across the membrane, whilst still in an unfolded conformation (Hartl et al., 1990; Arkowitz et al., 1993).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: A structure of the complete SecA-SecYEG complex has been determined with an ATP analogue (ADP-BeFx; PDB code 3DIN).
source: A structure of the complete SecA-SecYEG complex has been determined with an ATP analogue (ADP-BeFx; PDB code 3DIN)
evidence: This refers to a previously published crystal structure.

claim: A structure of the complete SecA-SecYEG complex has been determined with a short pre-protein mimic (PDB code 5EUL).
source: as well as with a short pre-protein mimic (Zimmer et al., 2008; Li et al., 2016) (PDB code 5EUL; modified in Figure 1a).
evidence: This refers to a previously published crystal structure.

claim: No structure of the ADP-bound state has been experimentally determined.
source: No structure of the ADP-bound state has been experimentally determined
evidence: This identifies a gap in structural knowledge based on the literature.

claim: Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations and Förster Resonance Energy Transfer (FRET) analyses suggest that ATP and ADP respectively favour open and closed forms of the SecY channel.
source: however, molecular dynamics (MD) simulations and Förster Resonance Energy Transfer (FRET) analyses suggest that ATP and ADP respectively favour open and closed forms of the SecY channel (Fessl et al., 2018; Allen et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior computational and experimental work.

claim: The behavior of ATP and ADP favoring open and closed forms of SecY was incorporated into a 'Brownian ratchet' model to describe the mechanism of ATP driven protein translocation.
source: This behaviour was incorporated into a 'Brownian ratchet' model to describe the mechanism of ATP driven protein translocation, whereby ATP binding and hydrolysis act to bias pre-protein diffusion in an outward direction.
evidence: This refers to a mechanistic model based on prior work.

claim: The directionality of the Brownian ratchet is further augmented by the promotion of pre-protein folding on the outside, but not the inside.
source: This directionality is further augmented by other factors, including the promotion of pre-protein folding on the outside, but not the inside (Corey et al., 2019)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The directionality of the Brownian ratchet is augmented by coupling transport to the trans-membrane proton-motive-force (PMF).
source: and by coupling transport to the trans-membrane proton-motive-force (PMF) (Brundage et al., 1990).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Non-hydrolysable ATP analogues cause the channel through SecY to open-up.
source: while they cause the channel through SecY to open-up (Allen et al., 2016)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Non-hydrolysable ATP analogues have been shown to prevent backsliding of trapped translocation intermediates.
source: they have also been shown to prevent backsliding of trapped translocation intermediates (Bauer et al., 2014; Erlandson et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: SecA is known to form a clamp for the translocating pre-protein.
source: Indeed, SecA is known to form a clamp for the translocating pre-protein (Zimmer et al., 2008)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The SecA clamp can be fixed in a closed state without preventing transport.
source: as the SecA clamp can be fixed in a closed state without preventing transport (Gold et al., 2013)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The conformational changes involved in SecA clamping are likely to be subtle, and not necessarily captured with techniques such as FRET.
source: the conformational changes involved are likely to be subtle, and not necessarily captured with techniques such as FRET.
evidence: This is an inference based on the limitations of FRET and prior experimental results.

claim: HDX-MS has emerged as a non-invasive and highly sensitive method for interrogating the conformational dynamics of membrane proteins and their complexes.
source: HDX-MS has emerged as a non-invasive and highly sensitive method for interrogating the conformational dynamics of membrane proteins and their complexes (Adhikary et al., 2017; Eisinger et al., 2017; Martens et al., 2018; Reading et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: HDX-MS measures the exchange of backbone amide hydrogen to deuterium at peptide-level resolution.
source: HDX-MS measures the exchange of backbone amide hydrogen to deuterium at peptide-level resolution (Englander and Kallenbach, 1983; Konermann et al., 2011; Engen, 2009).
evidence: This statement describes the fundamental principle of HDX-MS, supported by citations.

claim: The rate of HDX depends on the solvent accessibility, protein flexibility, and hydrogen bonding networks.
source: The rate of HDX depends on the solvent accessibility, protein flexibility, and hydrogen bonding networks (Mistarz et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: HDX-MS can monitor the conformational changes of protein complexes by comparing HDX rates between distinct protein states.
source: Thus, HDX-MS can monitor the conformational changes of protein complexes by comparing HDX rates between distinct protein states (e.g.. protein versus protein with ligand).
evidence: This describes the application of HDX-MS, supported by citation and knowledge.

claim: Comparative HDX-MS has emerged as an attractive tool to define conformational changes to complement other, high-resolution techniques.
source: Consequently, comparative HDX-MS has emerged as an attractive tool to define conformational changes to complement other, high-resolution techniques.
evidence: This is a general statement about the utility of HDX-MS in structural biology.

claim: The peptide coverage of the whole SecA-SecYEG complex was high (ranging from 82% to 95% for the respective subunits).
source: The peptide coverage of the whole complex was high (ranging from 82% to 95% for the respective subunits; Figure 2—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is a data quality metric from the HDX-MS experiments.

claim: There was very little effect of nucleotides on the conformational dynamics of the isolated SecA.
source: Surprisingly, there was very little effect on the conformational dynamics of the isolated SecA (Figure 2a,b and Figure 2—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This is a finding from the HDX-MS experiments comparing AMPPNP and ADP bound states of SecA alone.

claim: The greatest difference in deuterium uptake between the two nucleotide states of isolated SecA was observed at and around the ATP-binding sites.
source: The greatest difference in deuterium uptake between the two states was observed at and around the ATP-binding sites (Figure 2a,b).
evidence: This is a finding from the HDX-MS experiments on isolated SecA.

claim: SecA is only activated when it is associated with SecYEG.
source: This highlights the fact that SecA is only activated when it is associated with SecYEG
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the HDX-MS data showing minimal changes in isolated SecA.

claim: SecYEG induces a large ATP-dependent stabilisation across almost the entirety of SecA.
source: The results are consistent with SecYEG having a profound effect on SecA: SecYEG induces a large ATP-dependent stabilisation across almost the entirety of SecA (Figure 2c; negative ΔHDX, blue bars).
evidence: This is a finding from the HDX-MS experiments on the SecA-SecYEG complex.

claim: The presence of nucleotides conformationally activate SecA.
source: This implies that the presence of nucleotides conformationally activate SecA.
evidence: This is an inference from the HDX-MS data comparing SecA with and without SecYEG.

claim: The stabilised regions in SecA correspond with sites that directly contact the mature regions (PP-M) of the translocating pre-protein.
source: Most striking was the correspondence of the stabilised regions with sites in SecA that directly contact the mature regions (PP-M) of the translocating pre-protein (Figure 2a,c; dashed boxes –PP-M, grey bars).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the HDX-MS data in the context of the structural model.

claim: ATP-driven conformational closure of SecA around the mature segment of the pre-protein occurs.
source: Such stabilisation in SecA suggests an ATP-driven conformational closure around the mature segment of the pre-protein.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the HDX-MS data.

claim: The highlighted regions identified in SecA would be destabilised in the ADP-bound state, following ATP hydrolysis.
source: Conversely, of course, the highlighted regions identified in SecA would be destabilised in the ADP-bound state, following ATP hydrolysis.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the comparative HDX-MS data.

claim: Significant ATP-dependent destabilisation of SecY was found.
source: Interestingly, we found significant ATP-dependent destabilisation of SecY (Figure 3a,b, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the HDX-MS experiments on SecYEG in complex with SecA.

claim: Two prominently destabilised regions in SecY would be in direct contact with the signal sequence (PP-S) and mature regions (PP-M) of the pre-protein during protein translocation.
source: Closer inspection of the identified peptides reveals that two prominently destabilised regions in the SecY protein would be in direct contact with the signal sequence (PP-S) and mature regions (PP-M) of the pre-protein during protein translocation (Figure 3b; dashed boxes –PP-M grey, and PP-S yellow bars).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the HDX-MS data in the context of the structural model.

claim: The destabilised regions in SecY include the plug, which in the absence of the pre-protein maintains the closed state of the channel.
source: These regions include the plug, which in the absence of the pre-protein maintains the closed state of the channel (Van den Berg et al., 2004)
evidence: This statement combines HDX-MS findings with prior structural knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The destabilised regions in SecY include the highly conserved trans-membrane helix 7.
source: and the highly conserved trans-membrane helix 7.
evidence: This is part of the description of HDX-MS findings.

claim: Multiple regions within the SecE and SecG subunits were significantly destabilised in the presence of AMPPNP.
source: Multiple regions within the SecE and SecG subunits were also significantly destabilised in the presence of AMPPNP (Figure 3a,c–d and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the HDX-MS experiments.

claim: The identified regions in SecYEG would be stabilised after hydrolysis to ADP.
source: Again, conversely those identified regions would be stabilised after hydrolysis to ADP.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the comparative HDX-MS data.

claim: The observations are consistent with an ATP-driven opening of the SecY channel, and closure after hydrolysis.
source: These observations are consistent with an ATP-driven opening of the SecY channel, and closure after hydrolysis (Fessl et al., 2018; Allen et al., 2016).
evidence: This interpretation of the HDX-MS data is consistent with prior work cited.

claim: There is an ATP-dependent closure around the translocating polypeptide by SecA and opening of the channel through SecYEG.
source: Notably, there is an ATP-dependent closure around the translocating polypeptide by SecA and opening of the channel through SecYEG (Figure 4a)
evidence: This is a summary of the primary findings from the HDX-MS experiments.

claim: The ATP-dependent closure of SecA and opening of SecYEG is reversed in the ADP bound state after ATP hydrolysis.
source: reversed in the ADP bound state after ATP hydrolysis (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is a summary of the primary findings from the HDX-MS experiments.

claim: Both SecA pores contain residues shown by HDX-MS to be protected in the ATP-bound state.
source: note that both pores contain residues shown by HDX-MS to be protected in the ATP-bound state (Figure 2, Figure 4c and Materials and methods).
evidence: This connects the HDX-MS findings to the MD simulation analysis.

claim: Both SecA pores, particularly pore one at the cytoplasmic entrance of SecA, are more constricted in the ATP-bound state.
source: From the simulation data, it is clear that both SecA pores, particularly pore one at the cytoplasmic entrance of SecA, are more constricted in the ATP-bound state (Figure 4c,d).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of MD simulation data.

claim: ATP-binding is causing SecA to close around the engaged pre-protein.
source: This is consistent with the HDX data and suggests that ATP-binding is causing SecA to close around the engaged pre-protein.
evidence: This is an interpretation combining HDX-MS and MD simulation data.

claim: The results reveal profound nucleotide-dependent differences in the structure of the active Sec complex (SecA-SecYEG).
source: Overall, our results reveal profound nucleotide-dependent differences in the structure of the active Sec complex (SecA-SecYEG).
evidence: This is a summary statement of the primary findings.

claim: Regions affecting the membrane channel (SecY, SecE and SecG) become destabilised in the presence of ATP.
source: those affecting the membrane channel (SecY, SecE and SecG), which become destabilised in the presence of ATP
evidence: This is a summary of the HDX-MS findings.

claim: Regions affecting SecA become stabilised in the presence of ATP.
source: and those affecting SecA, which become stabilised.
evidence: This is a summary of the HDX-MS findings.

claim: The most dramatic changes affect regions that would directly contact a translocating pre-protein.
source: A more detailed analysis reveals that the most dramatic changes affect regions that would directly contact a translocating pre-protein.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the HDX-MS data in the context of the structural model.

claim: The results are consistent with the previously proposed Brownian ratchet mechanism of pre-protein transport.
source: These results are consistent with the previously proposed Brownian ratchet mechanism of pre-protein transport (Allen et al., 2016).
evidence: This connects the findings to prior mechanistic models.

claim: The cyclical ATP/ADP-dependent conformational dynamics highlighted in SecA and SecYEG are presumably integral components of the underling mechanism of the ratcheting machine.
source: The cyclical ATP/ADP-dependent conformational dynamics highlighted in SecA and SecYEG are presumably integral components of the underling mechanism of this ratcheting machine
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: The opening (ATP) and closure (ADP) of the channel through SecY is an integral component of the ratcheting mechanism.
source: for instance, the opening (ATP) and closure (ADP) of the channel through SecY (Corey et al., 2019).
evidence: This connects the findings to prior work on the mechanism.

claim: The conferral of ATP-dependent asymmetry that prevents pre-protein folding at the cytosolic side of the membrane, while allowing it at the exterior is likely to be a result of the observed conformational changes.
source: Secondly, the conferral of ATP-dependent asymmetry that prevents pre-protein folding at the cytosolic side of the membrane, while allowing it at the exterior (Corey et al., 2019) is likely to also be a result of these changes.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation connecting the findings to prior work.

claim: The observation that ATP causes SecA to constrict around the pre-protein could potentially explain why pre-proteins do not backslide in the presence of a non-hydrolysable ATP analogue.
source: Finally, the observation that ATP causes SecA to constrict around the pre-protein could potentially explain why pre-proteins do not backslide in the presence of a non-hydrolysable ATP analogue (Bauer et al., 2014; Erlandson et al., 2008)
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings in light of prior observations.

claim: The constriction of SecA around the pre-protein could promote forward transport.
source: and thereby promote forward transport.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the mechanistic implications.

claim: The experiments demonstrate the power of combining HDX-MS with the results of biochemistry and molecular simulations to understand the conformational mechanism of multi-component membrane protein complexes.
source: The experiments presented here demonstrate the power of combining HDX-MS with the results of biochemistry and molecular simulations to understand the conformational mechanism of multi-component membrane protein complexes, difficult to study by other approaches.
evidence: This is a general statement about the methodological approach of the study.

claim: AMPPNP was used to study the ATP-bound state because ATP is rapidly hydrolysed to ADP in the active complex.
source: AMPPNP was used to study the ATP-bound state because ATP is rapidly hydrolysed to ADP in the active complex
evidence: This explains the methodological choice based on biochemical knowledge.

claim: The peptide coverage ranged from 82% to 95% for the respective subunits of SecA-SecYEG.
source: The peptide coverage of the whole complex was high (ranging from 82% to 95% for the respective subunits; Figure 2—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is a data quality metric from the HDX-MS experiments.

claim: Pore 1 in SecA consists of residues Ile 222, Ser 224, Gly 326, Arg 327, Arg 328 and Ser 340 (in B. subtilis numbering).
source: Pore 1 consists of residues Ile 222, Ser 224, Gly 326, Arg 327, Arg 328 and Ser 340 (in B. subtilis numbering; equivalent to E. coli residues Ile 224, Ser 226, Gly 346, Arg 347, Arg 348 and Ser 350).
evidence: This describes the structural composition of pore 1 based on the MD simulation model.

claim: Pore 2 in SecA consists of Gln 595, Tyr 599 and Gln 736 on SecA, and Ile 243, Tyr 245 and Ala 246 on the C4 loop of SecY.
source: Pore 2 consists of Gln 595, Tyr 599 and Gln 736 on SecA (in B. subtilis numbering, E. coli equivalent are Gln 644, Tyr 648 and Gln 787), and Ile 243, Tyr 245 and Ala 246 on the functionally important (Corey et al., 2016b) C4 loop of SecY (G. thermodentrifinicans numbering, approximately equivalent to Val 246, Tyr 248 and Ala 249 on E. coli SecY).
evidence: This describes the structural composition of pore 2 based on the MD simulation model, with citation for functional importance.

claim: Residues Gly 346, Arg 347, Arg 348 and Ser 350 in pore one and Gln 787 and Ala 249 of pore 2 (all in E. coli numbering) are shown to be deprotected in the HDX data.
source: Note that residues Gly 346, Arg 347, Arg 348 and Ser 350 in pore one and Gln 787 and Ala 249 of pore 2 (all in E. coli numbering) are shown to be deprotected in the HDX data (see Data Availability).
evidence: This connects specific residues in the pores to the HDX-MS findings.

claim: Pore 1 means are 1.9 and 2.6 Å2 for ATP and ADP states respectively (p<0.0001).
source: both pores are tighter in ATP bound state (pore 1 means are 1.9 and 2.6 Å2, p<0.0001 using a 2 tailed t-test
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the MD simulation analysis with statistical support.

claim: Pore 2 means are 2.4 and 2.1 Å2 for ATP and ADP states respectively (p=0.0061).
source: pore 2 means are 2.4 and 2.1 Å2, p=0.0061).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the MD simulation analysis with statistical support.
